description: A diligent student with a strong background in theoretical CS and data structures in Python, but who feels intimidated by the transition to low-level C programming.

nodes.description: A foundational introduction to C-programming syntax and the Linux command line environment required for systems programming.
nodes.title: Introduction to Systems Programming in C
nodes.personalizationRationale: Provides essential background in C for a student with no_prior_exposure to the language before diving into kernel code.
Clarifies the hardware-software boundary for a student with no_prior_exposure to computer architecture concepts.
nodes.title: The Kernel/User Mode Distinction
nodes.description: Detailed exploration of the privilege separation between kernel mode and user mode, including how traps work.
Visualizing OS architecture by mapping software services like file management to the underlying hardware layer.
nodes.title: Visualizing OS Structures
nodes.personalizationRationale: Helps the student with no_prior_exposure build a mental model of how an operating system organizes its internal components.
Core curriculum node that summarizes foundational OS concepts required for all students.
nodes.title: Core OS Foundations and Services
nodes.description: An overview of standard operating system services, including system calls and the various types of system structures (monolithic vs microkernel).
Understanding the process abstraction, state transitions, and how the OS uses the Process Control Block (PCB) for management.
nodes.title: Process Management and Lifecycles
nodes.personalizationRationale: Fundamental concept required for the cumulative exam; focuses on the lifecycle of a process.

nodes.title: Inter-Process Communication Models
nodes.description: Comparing shared memory and message passing (sockets) as mechanisms for inter-process communication.
nodes.personalizationRationale: Covers required IPC mechanisms that will be used in future programming projects.
Essential thread theory required for all students to understand modern concurrency.
nodes.title: Threads and Threading Models
nodes.description: An analysis of user-level vs kernel-level threads and the use of threading libraries like Pthreads in systems development.

nodes.personalizationRationale: Core scheduling logic that is a primary focus of the midterm exam and course projects.
nodes.title: CPU Scheduling Algorithms
nodes.description: Comparative study of FCFS, Shortest-Job-First, Round Robin, and Priority scheduling algorithms.

nodes.personalizationRationale: Mandatory midterm assessment checkpoint to ensure the student is on track with the cumulative material.
nodes.description: A comprehensive review session and practice quiz covering the first five chapters of the textbook to prepare for the week 8 exam.
nodes.title: Midterm Progress Assessment (Ch. 1-5)

nodes.personalizationRationale: Critical synchronization concepts required for passing the final and completing project deliveries.
nodes.title: Process Synchronization Primitives
nodes.description: Solving the Critical Section problem using software and hardware primitives like Mutex locks and Semaphores.

nodes.personalizationRationale: Standard problems of concurrency that all students must be able to model analytically.
nodes.description: Practical application of synchronization tools to solve the Bounded-Buffer and Dining Philosophers problems.
nodes.title: Classic Synchronization Problems

nodes.personalizationRationale: A smaller but essential block covering deadlock theory required for the final exam.
nodes.description: Analyzing deadlock conditions (Coffman conditions) and applying the Banker's algorithm for avoidance and detection.
nodes.title: Deadlock Prevention and Avoidance

nodes.description: Physical memory management including contiguous allocation, fragmentation, and the structure of page tables.
nodes.title: Main Memory and Paging Structures
nodes.personalizationRationale: Core memory management theory which forms the basis for the final project delivery.

nodes.description: Advanced concepts in virtual memory, including demand paging and evaluating page replacement algorithms like LRU.
nodes.title: Virtual Memory and Page Replacement
nodes.personalizationRationale: Heavily weighted topic on the final exam; essential for understanding OS performance tradeoffs.

nodes.title: I/O Systems and Performance
nodes.description: Exploring the I/O subsystem architecture, including interrupt-driven I/O, DMA, and performance optimization.
nodes.personalizationRationale: Final block core content covering the hardware-software interface and storage performance.
Required material for the final cumulative examination covering file storage implementation.
nodes.title: File System Implementation
nodes.description: A deep dive into file system structures, directory implementation, and allocation methods like Indexed Allocation.
A cumulative final review session integrating all topics from the semester in preparation for the final exam.
nodes.title: Final Cumulative Course Review
nodes.personalizationRationale: Mandatory capstone assessment node to verify mastery of the entire syllabus.
